clue.text: Rogue charged seen in a dock endlessly

indicators.note: something seen in a word has been set down among its letters rather than joined on at either end

parts.note: a berth is a dock for a ship, and with 'a' in front the phrase loses its last letter and splits after four
a bull that charged you ran at you, so the past tense of run stands in

explanation.walkthrough: The surface builds a courtroom — a rogue charged, standing in the dock — and both of those words belong somewhere else entirely: the dock is a mooring.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogue -> ABERRANT: the sense in 'rogue gene' or 'rogue result', one that departs from the pattern it should follow.

clue.text: Whatever it takes from New York hobo and Cork boy

indicators.note: made new means made over again, and the capital lets the instruction hide inside what looks like a city's name

parts.note: eight letters of fodder, both words straight from the clue
seven more letters of fodder; Cork is a city and county in the south of Ireland

explanation.walkthrough: 'New York' reads as one place and is really two jobs: the first word is the instruction, the second is raw material, and the fifteen letters come out as one flat idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Whatever it takes -> BY HOOK OR BY CROOK: the idiom promises any means at all, fair or foul, which is what that phrase concedes.

clue.text: Recipe the last word in noodles

definitions.note: The answer is a mass noun naming one dish, so it takes a plural definition the way 'oats' or 'grits' would.

parts.note: R is the character a prescription opens with, from the Latin recipe, meaning 'take'
the word every prayer closes on, so having the last word is meant literally

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface is Japanese: it promises a cookery column having the final say, and the dish is assembled out of a prescription and a prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: noodles -> RAMEN: the Japanese wheat noodles served in broth, one particular kind standing in for the general word.

clue.text: Old canine somehow beginning to talk

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters get there by some unstated route, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so only the start of talk is used

parts.note: first letter of talk

explanation.surface: An elderly dog is, against the odds, starting to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'canine' the dog in the picture, but it is fodder: 'beginning to' takes T from talk, and the indicator after canine mixes those six letters plus T.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient means very old, of great age, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Temperature lowered initially in America's city

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: USA is the abbreviation for the United States of America

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so take the first letter of lowered

parts.note: first letter of lowered

explanation.surface: The thermometer readings dropped early on in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' takes L from 'lowered', and 'in' sets it inside USA to give ULSA, which follows T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tulsa is a city in Oklahoma, in the United States.

clue.text: Weary Willies pee in streetcars

indicators.note: a letter that goes in a word is dropped among its letters, not added at one end

parts.note: streetcars is the American word; the British one is five letters that open up before the last
the letter written the way its name is spelled

explanation.walkthrough: Weary Willie and Tired Tim were vagrants in an old British comic strip, which is why the definition arrives looking like two men's names.
explanation.definitionFit: Weary Willies -> TRAMPS: a Weary Willie is a footsore vagrant, so the plural names the men who walk the roads.

clue.text: Drake's outside drawn into coach deal

indicators.note: something drawn into another is pulled inside it

parts.note: a coach is a railway carriage, and a train is a set of them; in Britain coach also means train-like transport

indicators.note: the outside of a word is its first and last letters

parts.note: the name Drake, in its possessive form, whose letters are then trimmed

explanation.surface: A rapper's exterior has been sketched into a business arrangement over a coach.
explanation.walkthrough: Drake here is just a name to trim: its 'outside' is DE, which is 'drawn into' the railway word for coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade-in is a deal in which an old item is handed over as part-payment for a new one.

clue.text: Declaration FIFA put out: Stateside lawyer against it

indicators.note: put out means disturbed or upset, so the governing body's letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written
a DA is a district attorney, a public prosecutor in the United States
V, for versus, means against

explanation.surface: Football's world governing body issues a statement, and an American attorney opposes it.
explanation.walkthrough: Only FIFA is mixed up, by 'put out', giving AFFI; the rest is a straight run of DA, V and IT.
explanation.definitionFit: An affidavit is a written statement sworn on oath, a formal declaration used as evidence.

clue.text: Mona Lisa in novel form?

definitions.meaning: Leonardo painted one woman, half-length, and what hangs in the Louvre is exactly what these four words describe
Henry James published a book under that same string of words in 1881

explanation.walkthrough: The italics are the tell that a title is being quoted, and the clue asks you to carry the same words off a gallery wall and onto a shelf of fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Mona Lisa -> PORTRAIT OF A LADY: definition by example, the most famous one ever painted; novel -> the Henry James book of that title.

clue.text: Toxic campaign in Africa where calm disrupted

indicators.note: something disrupted has been broken up and put back out of true, which is what becomes of the letters

parts.note: fifteen letters of fodder, three words taken straight from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: 'In Africa' reads as the place the campaign happened, so the continent looks like scene-setting; it is fodder, and 'in' is the only word here that carries nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Toxic campaign -> CHEMICAL WARFARE: fighting with gas and nerve agents, so the campaign itself is the poisonous thing.

clue.text: Urban resident to admit severing link

indicators.note: to sever something is to cut it clean in two, and the halves of the cut word close again around whatever went between

parts.note: a tie is a link between two people, three letters cut after the first
to own up to something is to admit it

explanation.walkthrough: 'To admit' looks like a plain infinitive holding the sentence upright; only the 'to' is doing that, and the verb after it is already fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Urban resident -> TOWNIE: someone who lives in the town, as country people or students say it of the locals.

clue.text: English road taken through a bleak Welsh town

indicators.note: 'taken through' puts the English road pieces inside the word for bleak

parts.note: bare means bleak and empty, as of a landscape

explanation.surface: An English road runs across a desolate landscape to a town in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberdare is a former mining town in the Cynon Valley in South Wales.

clue.text: Amateur player from insanely rich nation

indicators.note: to do a thing insanely is to do it without order or reason, and letters handled without order arrive rearranged

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, both words straight from the clue

explanation.walkthrough: Corinthian-Casuals still play in the English leagues, and the club's name is why the word came to stand for sport played for its own sake.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateur player -> CORINTHIAN: a gentleman sportsman who competes for love of the game, the sense behind 'the Corinthian spirit'.

clue.text: Facial make-up used by the police?

definitions.meaning: the surface offers cosmetics; read it the other way and make-up is what a thing is made up of, the parts a face is composed from
detectives build a suspect's face to a witness's description, picking eyes, nose and chin out of a stock set

explanation.walkthrough: It began as a trade name and slipped into ordinary English the way Hoover did, which is why the answer looks like a common noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue -> IDENTIKIT: a composite face assembled from standard features, so 'make-up' means composition rather than cosmetics.

clue.text: Bad practice where doctor dismissed

indicators.note: a man dismissed is sent away from the place, and the letters that stand for him go with him

parts.note: a drill is a practice run, the sort a fire alarm or a squad does
Dr is the standard abbreviation, and this is the pair that leaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad practice' reads as one phrase, close to malpractice, which keeps the surface honest about doctors; the parse wants the second word on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Bad -> ILL: the sense in 'ill will' or 'ill-advised', where it means bad rather than unwell.

clue.text: Ego in goods vehicle always looking in mirror

indicators.note: a letter put in a vehicle rides inside it, landing between its letters rather than alongside

parts.note: the small lorry that carries goods, three letters that open up before the last
the ego is the self, and ego is simply Latin for 'I'

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a picture rather than a synonym, and it starts in the middle of what still reads as one sentence about a driver.
explanation.definitionFit: always looking in mirror -> VAIN: too pleased with your own appearance to pass a reflection without checking it.

clue.text: Clever message concealing its opening

indicators.note: a word concealing something keeps it out of sight, so the letter named is never written down

parts.note: a cable is a message sent by telegraph, five letters with one to lose
the letter that message word opens with, kept out of sight

explanation.walkthrough: 'Concealing' tempts you to go hunting for letters buried in the clue; what it hides here is a single letter of the message, which simply goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Clever -> ABLE: competent and capable, the practical kind of clever that a school report means.

clue.text: Readiness to eat shown by one in safety

indicators.note: a letter dropped in a word lands among its letters instead of at one end

parts.note: being saved is safety in the religious sense, nine letters that part after three
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shown by' is pure joinery, asserting nothing except that the two halves of the clue are the same thing, and beginners lose time looking for a mechanism in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Readiness to eat -> SALIVATION: the mouth watering at the sight of food, the body's own signal that it is ready for a meal.

clue.text: Employee in post about to be recalled

parts.note: a staff is a pole or post

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: re means about, concerning, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A worker in a job is about to be called back by the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post' suggests a job, but here it is a pole; 'about' is not 'nearly' but RE, which 'to be recalled' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: A staffer is a member of staff, a person employed by an organisation.

clue.text: Animal doctor worked near warhorse

parts.note: a vet is a veterinary surgeon, a doctor for animals

indicators.note: worked as in worked over, kneaded, so the letters of near are reshaped

explanation.surface: The vet treated an animal close to an old war horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'warhorse' reads as a cavalry animal, but it is used figuratively for an old campaigner.
explanation.definitionFit: An old warhorse is someone with long experience of a field, a seasoned veteran.

clue.text: Bed left in smooth state once

indicators.note: pieces set in a word are laid down between its letters, splitting it open to take them

parts.note: to sand a surface is to smooth it, and the four letters part after the first
a cot is a child's bed
L is the standard abbreviation for left, as on a map or a boot

explanation.walkthrough: It was an independent kingdom until the Union with England in 1707, and that history is the whole job of 'once' at the end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: state once -> SCOTLAND: sovereign until 1707 and since then a nation inside the United Kingdom rather than a state of its own.

clue.text: Reasonable belief in beatitude is misplaced

indicators.note: the little word says the answer is already sitting in what follows, to be found there rather than built

parts.note: five consecutive letters run out of the end of the first word, across the second and into the third

explanation.walkthrough: 'Misplaced' looks like an instruction to shuffle everything in front of it; it is only the last word of the hiding place, and nothing moves at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Reasonable belief -> DEISM: belief in a creator arrived at by reason alone, with no revelation or scripture behind it.

clue.text: Support from AA where drinker heads without whiskey

indicators.note: the word still carries its old sense of 'outside', so what it names is left outside and the rest closes round it

parts.note: a drinker heads to the bar, and those five letters break apart at the join between the words
whiskey is W in the NATO alphabet that radio operators spell with

explanation.walkthrough: The AA is Britain's Automobile Association, whose patrols tow broken-down cars away — and the surface quietly lets you read it as Alcoholics Anonymous instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Support from AA -> TOW BAR: the fitting bolted to a car so a recovery service can hitch on and pull it.

clue.text: Social realist in healthy society

parts.note: someone healthy is in good health
S is the abbreviation for society, the one a club puts in its initials

explanation.walkthrough: H.G. Wells is remembered for the time machine and the Martians, but he also wrote closely observed novels of shop assistants and clerks, which is the side the definition takes.
explanation.definitionFit: Social realist -> WELLS: H.G. Wells, whose Kipps and Mr Polly document lower-middle-class English life with documentary sharpness.

clue.text: Surprise move for big wedding venue in European location

parts.note: to rock someone is to shock or surprise them

indicators.note: move here means shift around, so the letters of for big are rearranged

parts.note: a church wedding takes place at the altar

explanation.surface: A sudden decision to hold a lavish wedding somewhere on the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: Gibraltar is a British territory on Spain's south coast; 'Surprise' is a verb in disguise, as to rock someone is to shock them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rock of Gibraltar is a limestone promontory at the southern tip of Iberia, so a place in Europe.

clue.text: Fish by river: one to glide across frozen surface

definitions.text: one to glide across frozen surface

parts.note: a flat cartilaginous sea fish, a close relative of the ray
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.walkthrough: The colon is the setter marking his own seam: everything before it is wordplay, everything after it is the definition, and 'by' does the joining.
explanation.definitionFit: one to glide across frozen surface -> SKATER: a person on blades, carried over the ice of a rink or a frozen lake.

clue.text: Object to view around yard in contemplation

definitions.note: The answer is a noun phrase while the definition is adverbial: the setter defines the idiom as it is used, since what you see in your mind's eye you see in contemplation.

parts.note: if you mind something you object to it, as in 'do you mind?'

indicators.note: a word set around a letter closes over it, so the letter finishes up between its own

parts.note: to view is to see, and the three letters part before the last
y is the abbreviation for the imperial yard

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has someone peering over a fence at a garden, and not one word of it is scenery: every piece hands over letters and 'in' is the only join.
explanation.definitionFit: in contemplation -> MIND'S EYE: the inward view, where you picture a thing rather than look at it.
